planting.note: Direct sow after the soil has warmed, or start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost for earlier bloom; established plants self-sow readily.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained garden soil in full sun; hollyhock mallow produces upright, bushy clumps of deeply lobed foliage topped with saucer-shaped, soft pink flowers resembling small hollyhocks from midsummer into fall. Unlike true hollyhocks, it is rarely bothered by rust and holds a tidy, bushy habit without staking. Deadhead spent stems to tidy the clump and curb excessive self-sowing. It combines well with ornamental grasses and other cottage-garden perennials in a sunny mixed border.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, since germination is slow and uneven; set divisions or transplants out after frost danger passes in well-drained soil.

directions: Plant in average to fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot climates; Nepal cinquefoil forms a loose, spreading mound of strawberry-like leaflets with wiry, branching stems carrying rose-pink, saucer-shaped flowers with a darker eye from early to midsummer. It is the parent species behind many popular garden hybrids but is itself a reliable, long-blooming border perennial. Shear lightly after the first flush to encourage rebloom, and divide clumps every two to three years to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; set out divisions or transplants after frost in well-drained soil amended with grit on heavy sites.

directions: Plant in lean to average, sharply drained soil in full sun; Himalayan cinquefoil forms a low mound of silvery-green, palmate leaflets with wiry stems bearing deep blood-red to brick-red, five-petaled flowers through summer. It is one of the parent species of many garden hybrid potentillas and tolerates heat and drought once established better than richer, moisture-loving perennials. Avoid overly rich, moist soil, which encourages lax growth and reduces flowering; good drainage over winter is essential for longevity.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, or sow direct in fall; set transplants out after frost in well-drained soil.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot regions; Pyrenees daisy sends up sturdy stems topped with large, single white daisy flowers with a bright yellow center from early to midsummer, held above a basal clump of glossy, leathery, toothed leaves. It is one of the wild parent species behind the popular Shasta daisy hybrids and shares their reliable garden performance. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigorous, free-flowering growth.

planting.note: Seed benefits from a cold, moist stratification period before sowing indoors; set out divisions or transplants in gritty, well-drained soil after the last frost.

directions: Plant in lean, sharply drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; cliff anemone is a tough North American native forming a low tuft of finely divided, silky-hairy foliage with wiry stems carrying cream to brick-red or dusky rose flowers in late spring and early summer, followed by fluffy, cottony seed heads. It thrives in rocky, exposed sites and resents winter wet far more than cold, making excellent drainage essential. Suited to rock gardens, alpine troughs, and dry native plantings at higher elevations or northern latitudes.

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring or fall into lean, well-drained soil; seedlings establish slowly the first year before flowering in the second season.

directions: Plant in lean to average, well-drained, alkaline-tolerant soil in full sun; greater knapweed produces deeply cut, grayish-green leaves and branching stems topped with large, thistle-like reddish-purple flowerheads with conspicuously fringed outer florets from midsummer into fall. It is an outstanding nectar source for bees and butterflies and tolerates poor, chalky, or dry soils better than richer garden ground. Allow spent heads to stand for seed-eating birds, and cut back in late fall to tidy the planting.

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring, or start indoors 6 weeks before the last frost for earlier bloom; plants form a basal rosette the first year.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; giant knapweed forms a coarse clump of large, bristly leaves and sturdy stems topped with oversized, golden-yellow thistle flowers emerging from distinctive brown, papery, scale-covered buds that resemble a pine cone before opening. The large flowerheads are prized fresh and dried for cutting and are a strong draw for bees and butterflies. Stake in exposed sites, as the heavy flowerheads can lodge the tall stems in wind and rain.
